messages.subject: generated quantities??
parts:
Hi all. Following the example on p.91 of the Stan manual, I added the following lines to my 8-schools model:

generated quantities {
real y_rep[J];
for (j in 1:J)
y_rep[j] <- rand_normal (0,1);
}

I got the following error:

TRANSLATING MODEL 'anon_model' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name, :
failed to parse Stan model 'anon_model' and error message provided as:
LOCATION: file=input; line=19, column=36

y_rep[j] <- rand_normal (0,1);
^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

no matches for function name="rand_normal"
arg 0 type=int
arg 1 type=int
expression is ill formed
Parser expecting: <eps>


(And changing 0 and 1 to 0. and 1. did not fix it, it just changed the arguments to real and gave the same error.)

It also failed when I made y_rep a simple scalar and when I replaced rand_normal by normal.

What am I doing wrong??? I know it's something stupid...

Thanks.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: rand_normal doesn't exist
parts:
Sorry. My bad.

The error message that Andrew got below is right.
The doc is wrong. So far, we haven't implemented rand_normal,
so this code won't work:

> generated quantities {
> real y_rep[J];
> for (j in 1:J)
> y_rep[j] <- rand_normal (0,1);
> }

It's the next feature I'm going to add, but it
may take a bit to push it through all 30 or
so distributions. I laid some of the groundwork before
1.0.0, so it's not that much work from here.

Daniel's already working on vectorizations for the
rest of the probability functions, too. When both are
done, it'll simplify the manual. For now, I'm also
going to take Ben's advice of adding a table indicating
which probability functions have been vectorized.
(And to enrich the error messages indicating which
signatures ARE available.)

I'll take the references to it out of the manual,
which I'm about to update w.r.t. Andrew's other
comments.

This is the problem with a 200-ish page manual -- it's
hard to keep giving it a complete proofread. I
should stick to never adding things to the manual
until I add them to the code.

- Bob

messages.subject: naming prob and cdf functions?
parts:
While we're on the topic of naming, what
convention should we use?

I actually prefer

random_normal()

to rand_normal(), but given that it doesn't exist, we can call it
anything. (I read too much C++ code these days, which
has the convention of aggressively abbreviating identifiers.)

I'm thinking we should add aliases (and deprecate
the old versions) for the CDF functions. I
like

normal_cdf()

better than normal_p() which is what's in there now.
I was following the R convention in a half-assed way.
It'll also let us implement *_ccdf() for the complementary
functions, which can be important for numerical
stability (though maybe we could figure that out under
the hood and not bother the user).

- Bob

quantities block?

I.E.,

y ~ normal(0,1)

gets translated to

y = random_normal(0,1);

Hence the (non C++) user never really sees rand_normal or random_normal.

Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] naming prob and cdf functions?
parts: On 8/31/12 2:08 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:> Weren't we also planning to use the ~ notation for the generated

> quantities block?
>
> I.E.,
>
> y ~ normal(0,1)
>
> gets translated to
>
> y = random_normal(0,1);
>
> Hence the (non C++) user never really sees rand_normal or random_normal.

Excellent point. And if we do that, we won't even
need to make random_normal() accessible as a regular
function elsewhere, which is convenient, because it
requires a reference to the sampler's RNG if we're
going to have seeds fully determine runs.

So unless anyone objects, the plan will be to do as
Marcus outlines above.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] naming prob and cdf functions?
parts:
1. I agree that random_normal is better than rand_normal.

2. Earlier, I'd liked the idea that y ~ normal (0,1) in the generated quantities block gets translated into y <- random_normal (0,1).

But now I have mixed feelings. Now that I fully understand that "~" maps directly into a log-probability statement, I'm not so happy about overloading the "~" symbol so that it means different things in different blocks of the program.

One difficulty I think we're _always_ going to have with users (including me) is confusion between ~ and <-. Back when I wrote Bugs code, I was always typing <- for ~ or vice-versa.

I have the impression that for a stan model, that any expression can be ~ or <- but not both. That is, depending on declarations, if the statement
foo1 <- foo2
is correct, then
foo1 ~ foo2
is incorrect. And vice-versa. So in fact the choice of "~" or "<-" is in fact a piece of redundant information. That's ok, a bit of redundancy is ok. In any case, I'm pretty sure that when I write Stan models I will continue to use ~ instead of <- and vice-versa. It's just hard to keep straight.

A

On Fri, Aug 31, 2012 at 5:12 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> 1. I agree that random_normal is better than rand_normal.

Thinking about it more, I would also propose normal_random to be
consistent with normal_log, normal_cdf etc.

>
> 2. Earlier, I'd liked the idea that y ~ normal (0,1) in the generated quantities block gets translated into y <- random_normal (0,1).
>
> But now I have mixed feelings. Now that I fully understand that "~" maps directly into a log-probability statement, I'm not so happy about overloading the "~" symbol so that it means different things in different blocks of the program.
>
> One difficulty I think we're _always_ going to have with users (including me) is confusion between ~ and <-. Back when I wrote Bugs code, I was always typing <- for ~ or vice-versa.
>
> I have the impression that for a stan model, that any expression can be ~ or <- but not both. That is, depending on declarations, if the statement
> foo1 <- foo2
> is correct, then
> foo1 ~ foo2
> is incorrect. And vice-versa. So in fact the choice of "~" or "<-" is in fact a piece of redundant information. That's ok, a bit of redundancy is ok. In any case, I'm pretty sure that when I write Stan models I will continue to use ~ instead of <- and vice-versa. It's just hard to keep straight.

In the model block

foo1 <- foo2(a,b)

is not the same as

foo1 ~ foo2(a,b)

The first means assignment of a value (i.e., in C++ foo1 = foo2(a,b);)
while the second declares something as being distributed according to
a distribution. The second gets translated into:

lp__ += foo2_log(foo1,a,b);

I prefer overloading ~ because it has an intuitive match to a commonly
used notation. In the generated quantities block the second statement
would become something like:

random_normal(foo1,a,b);

Note that this does imply a restricted statement syntax for the LHS of
a ~ in the generated quantities block. I suppose that's the one
advantage of using <- in generated quantities because that rule would
be consistent.

Cheers,
Marcus

>
> A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] naming prob and cdf functions?
parts:
On 8/31/12 5:49 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> On Fri, Aug 31, 2012 at 5:12 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>> 1. I agree that random_normal is better than rand_normal.
>
> Thinking about it more, I would also propose normal_random to be
> consistent with normal_log, normal_cdf etc.

Yup. That makes sense to me.

How do people feel about normal_cdf() vs. normal_p()?

Again, at this point, renaming is a pain, as we'd
want to add normal_cdf() and deprecate normal_p().

>> 2. Earlier, I'd liked the idea that y ~ normal (0,1) in the generated quantities block gets translated into y <- random_normal (0,1).
>>
>> But now I have mixed feelings. Now that I fully understand that "~" maps directly into a log-probability statement, I'm not so happy about overloading the "~" symbol so that it means different things in different blocks of the program.
>>
>> One difficulty I think we're _always_ going to have with users (including me) is confusion between ~ and <-. Back when I wrote Bugs code, I was always typing <- for ~ or vice-versa.

Odd. That's one confusion I never had. But then
I'm a programming language type freak and I knew
how these operations were implemented in updates.

My problem is that I keep trying to use the equal
sign for assignment everywhere. The use of <- seems
restricted to R and its syntactic descendants,
BUGS, JAGS, and now Stan.

>> I have the impression that for a stan model, that any expression can be ~ or <- but not both. That is, depending on declarations, if the statement
>> foo1 <- foo2
>> is correct, then
>> foo1 ~ foo2
>> is incorrect.

There's nowhere at the moment that both of those
would be legal, because the right side of ~ needs to be
a distribution name and parameters and the
right side of <- needs to be a general expression.

x ~ foo(a,b,c); ===> lp__ += foo_log(x,a,b,c);

x <- foo(a,b,c); ===> x = foo(a,b,c);

There is no foo such that both foo_log() and foo() is
a function, so there's no foo where both are well defined.

> And vice-versa. So in fact the choice of "~" or "<-" is in fact a piece of redundant information.
> That's ok, a bit of redundancy is ok. In any case, I'm pretty sure that when
> I write Stan models I will continue to use ~ instead of <- and vice-versa. It's just hard to keep straight.
>
> In the model block
>
> foo1 <- foo2(a,b)
>
> is not the same as
>
> foo1 ~ foo2(a,b)
>
> The first means assignment of a value (i.e., in C++ foo1 = foo2(a,b);)
> while the second declares something as being distributed according to
> a distribution. The second gets translated into:
>
> lp__ += foo2_log(foo1,a,b);
>
> I prefer overloading ~ because it has an intuitive match to a commonly
> used notation. In the generated quantities block the second statement
> would become something like:
>
> random_normal(foo1,a,b);
>
> Note that this does imply a restricted statement syntax for the LHS of
> a ~ in the generated quantities block.

Good point. The a in a ~ will need to be assignable (aka an lvalue).

I can just test that the a is assignable (aka an lvalue) by
attaching a semantic action to the rule that only fires in

the generated quantities block.

> I suppose that's the one
> advantage of using <- in generated quantities because that rule would
> be consistent.

It would certainly be easier.

But then you get an inconsistency that you have a function
random_normal() that can only be applied in the generated
quantities block.

A halfway approach would be to treat normal(mu,sigma) as a function
that returns a normal variate. So you could have

y_rep <- normal(mu,sigma);

in the generated quantities block. But then we're back to
functions that only exist in one block.

Recall that we decided to not go with random functions in the data block.
It would seriously complicate the design, because up until now,
the data gets assigned once and reused for multiple chains. If that
were the interpretation we wanted, it'd be easy enough. But there's
really no good way to output variables from the transformed data block
anyway.

It might be possible to use some randomization inside other
loops in the tansformed params or params, but then it would
get executed once per leapfrog step.

But the more I think about it, the more I like just overloading
with a side test that the LHS is an lvalue.

- Bob
